newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zaire rebel takeover could spark big mining business.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebel takeover could spark big mining business.

text.p: Zaire's mining industry may get a much-needed boost and begin realising its vast potential after Laurent Kabila's rebels ousted president Mobutu Sese Seko, analysts said on Monday.

The central African country is regarded as one of the richest mineral areas in the world still to be explored but the mining industry -- once the world's largest copper exporter -- sank into decline under Mobutu's rule.
"It is a country that needs to be brought back from the brink," said Johannesburg-based metals analyst Stephen Briggs, of stockbrockers EW Balderson.
Foreign exchange earnings from the country's copper, cobalt, diamond and gold mines were hardly ever reinvested in the mines, making mining almost impossible in some areas.
Zaire's vast copper and cobalt wealth is concentrated in Shaba province, which is also Kabila's home province.
Diamonds from Kasai province made Zaire the world's second largest producer by volume in 1995 after Australia and it was also the fourth-largest gold producer in Africa.

In the mid-1980s Zaire produced some 500,000 tonnes of copper a year but last year output was only 40,000 tonnes. Cobalt output has dropped from 15,000 to around 4,000 tonnes, although this still represents a fifth of world production.
Analysts said with a new government in Kinshasa and Kabila seen as a pragmatist who realises the need for foreign investment, Zaire's mining industry could be set for a re-birth.
"The bottom line is that there are huge resources there, waiting to be exploited.
"Some of them are world class and will attract the foreign investment that will allow them to be exploited," said Jim Lennon, metals analyst at Macquarie Equities in London.
Foreign companies like Tenke Mining Corp and America Mineral Fields (AMF) are already poised to sink millions of dollars into copper, cobalt and zinc mines in Shaba province.
In April, AMF won the rights to the Kolwezi copper/cobalt tailings project and to build a 200,000 tonnes a year zinc plant at Kipushi.

The U.S.-based company was the first to be awarded a project by Kabila's rebels -- a move which incensed South African mining giant Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd which had earlier submitted a rival bid to Zaire's state mining company Gecamines.
Lennon said he believed more foreign investment would begin flowing into Zaire in the near future.
"There will be this eventual freeing up of overseas investment capital that will go into Zaire. I don't think there are going to be any short-term changes, nothing overnight".

"I think that you've got to be optimistic, that there will be the availability of more investment funds from a wider variety of sources, from international agencies and U.S. government sources and also the Europeans," he said.
Briggs said foreign firms would regard the change in Zaire's leadership favourably.
"They can now presumably start serious talking. Before the rebels took Kinshasa, nobody seemed to know how Mobutu and his acolytes would behave.
"They can get down to the serious business of arguing about how much they've got to pay for these deposits," Briggs said.
International companies have beaten a path to Kabila's headquarters in the southern copper mining city of Lumbumbashi since early April to seek a slice of Zaire's business prospects.
Lennon said the international community would have sympathy for Zaire's efforts to rebuild its mines.
"I think that there will be tremendous sympathy for Zaire to rebuild, because it (the mining industry) is the one source of competitive advantage that they've got," he added.
